title: Pytest-friendly Test API
text:
Issue #5683: Pytest-friendly Test API
Labels: type:enhancement, area:debugging

Streamlit is phenomenal. Everyone knows this. This is why [my beautiful science wife](https://www.researchgate.net/profile/Alexis-Pietak) <sup>:heart_eyes_cat: </sup> and I are building out our next [open-source multiphysics bioelectricity simulator](https://github.com/betsee/betse) in Streamlit.

Streamlit: *yup, it even does bioelectricity.*

## Streamlit Testing: A Chink in the Armour

But all is not quite so phenomenal on the testing front. Sadly, Streamlit currently offers *no* official means of testing Streamlit apps from a `pytest` test suite. Technically, there does exist:

* **A [third-party `streamlit-mock` package](https://github.com/acschofield/streamlit_mock).** Of course, this package is effectively unmaintained. While we applaud the one lone GitHub user brave enough to star `streamlit-mock`, we are not that user. 
* **Browser-based automation ala Cyprus and Selenium.** Of course, then *we* would have to develop, debug, and maintain non-trivial end-to-end WebDriver tests renowned for  [superficially behaving non-deterministically](https://salmonmode.github.io/2020/05/11/is-selenium-flaky.html) in perpetuity. Grant funding only extends so far. It doesn't extend that far. Which is probably good, because we value our sanity and marital stability.

## streamlit-mock: Visions of a Better Future

Nobody should use `streamlit-mock`, because nobody should use unmaintained things. But everybody should be *inspired* by `streamlit-mock` to create something similar that actually works and is well-maintained, because the core conceits behind `streamlit-mock` are sound. To [quote their `README.md`](https://github.com/acschofield/streamlit_mock/blob/main/README.md):

title: Pytest-friendly Test API
text:
Nobody should use `streamlit-mock`, because nobody should use unmaintained things. But everybody should be *inspired* by `streamlit-mock` to create something similar that actually works and is well-maintained, because the core conceits behind `streamlit-mock` are sound. To [quote their `README.md`](https://github.com/acschofield/streamlit_mock/blob/main/README.md):

> Our simple streamlit application calling a REST API backend grew over time, became not so simple and needed a test suite. We wrote some Selenium tests, but these are tricky to get right and run relatively slowly. This package "mocks" most streamlit class to allow "pytest" to be used for testing.

> Goals:
> * **Allow tests to be written using pytest**
> * **Tests should run quickly** so that multiple edge cases and variants can be tested
> * **Tests should be concise and easy to write**

> Non-Goals:
> * Testing streamlit itself (the package removes all dependnecies on the real streamlitk)
> * Testing that the app uses Streamlit correctly (the package fakes input and records outputs)
> * To be as complete as an end-to-end Selenium test (Streamlit/web server are out of the loop)

Goals seem reasonable. Non-goals seem reasonable, too. We applaud these reasonable things.

## What Do You Want Us to Do About Your Problems, Bro?

title: Pytest-friendly Test API
text:
Goals seem reasonable. Non-goals seem reasonable, too. We applaud these reasonable things.

## What Do You Want Us to Do About Your Problems, Bro?

**Okay.** Let's get down to brass data science tacks. It'd be phenomenal if Streamlit itself offered an official `pytest`-friendly test API – lightly inspired by `streamlit_mock` but actually well-maintained and working. An official `github.com/streamlit/pytest-streamlit` plugin trivially enabling Streamlit apps to be tested under `pytest` would be *especially* phenomenal. `pytest-streamlit` would hypothetically provide support – presumably in the form of one or more `pytest` fixtures – for programmatically running *any* arbitrary Streamlit app as an integration test under a Streamlit mock API.

Indeed, we see that [Streamlit itself tests itself with a `pytest` test suite](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/develop/lib/tests/streamlit/runtime/scriptrunner/script_runner_test.py). This sorta suggests that the requisite functionality for testing downstream Streamlit apps with `pytest` already exists... *within Streamlit itself*! Shock twist is shocking. :open_mouth: 

Indeed, we see that [the existing `streamlit/lib/tests/streamlit/runtime/scriptrunner/script_runner_test.py` integration test](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/develop/lib/tests/streamlit/runtime/scriptrunner/script_runner_test.py) appears to already be doing most – maybe even all – of the heavy lifting we'd expect from an official `github.com/streamlit/pytest-streamlit` plugin.

Copy-and-pasting the deeply nested functionality of `script_runner_test.py` into our own `pytest` test suite justifiably frightens us, however. If something resembling that could be published as a stand-alone API for reuse by the general public, we will happily dance with our Maine Coon cats on the frozen lake outside our cottage in a TikTok video generally regarded as deplorable.

## What We Used to Do No Longer Works, Which Is Sad

title: Pytest-friendly Test API
text:
## What We Used to Do No Longer Works, Which Is Sad

Previously, we used to exercise our entire Streamlit app with a trivial integration test in our `pytest` test suite resembling:

```python
def test_app_lifecycle(capsys) -> None:
    '''
    Integration test exercising the **maximally trivial app lifecycle** (i.e.,
    workflow spinning up, running, and then immediately shutting down this app).

    Parameters
    ----------
    capsys
        Builtin fixture object permitting pytest-specific capturing (i.e.,
        hiding) of both standard output and error to be temporarily disabled.
    '''

    # Temporarily disable pytest-specific capturing (i.e., hiding) of both
    # standard output and error for the duration of this integration test. Why?
    # Because this test often takes an excessive amount of time and can,
    # moreover, fail to halt in various edge cases outside our control.
    # Capturing output unhelpfully obscures these concerns during local testing.
    with capsys.disabled():
        # Defer test-specific imports.
        #
        # Note that:
        # * Importing "hot_bioelectricity_app.main" has the beneficial side
        #   effect of running this Streamlit-based web app to completion.
        # * Attempting to run this app via the "streamlit run" subcommand does
        #   *NOT* halt as expected, as that subcommand understandably runs the
        #   passed app indefinitely.
        from hot_bioelectricity_app import main

        # Immediately return after doing so.
        return
```

### Summary

Hi,

I am running a Streamlit app on Azure, requiring authentication with AD, and `st.file_uploader` returns a 403 Forbidden error if `enableXsrfProtection` is on. It works locally, and I suspect that this is caused by the _xsrf cookie not getting though, because I can see the cookie in dev tools locally, but not when deployed.

In particular, the cookie is missing the SameSite and Secure attributes.

### Reproducible Code Example

_No response_

### Steps To Reproduce

1. Open any Streamlit app
2. Open browser developer tools

### Expected Behavior

Cookies have `SameSite=None; Secure` attribute.

### Current Behavior

_xsrf cookie is not transmitted when deployed on the cloud with SSO and HTTPS-only.

Locally this is what I am getting:

>Some cookies are misusing the recommended “SameSite“ attribute

This means that the cookie will no longer be sent in third-party contexts. If your application depends on this cookie being available in such contexts, please add the “SameSite=None“ attribute to it. To know more about the “SameSite“ attribute, read https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Set-Cookie/SameSite

[CONTRIBUTOR] This issue reports that the `_xsrf` (XSRF/CSRF protection) cookie is missing the `SameSite=None; Secure` attributes, which causes `st.file_uploader` to return 403 Forbidden errors when Streamlit apps are deployed behind reverse proxies, SSO authentication (like Azure AD), or embedded in iframes. Modern browsers require `SameSite=None; Secure` for cookies to be transmitted in cross-origin contexts.

**Root Cause Analysis:** The XSRF cookie is set in `lib/streamlit/web/server/routes.py` (line 202-206) using `self.set_cookie()`, but the `xsrf_cookie_kwargs` dictionary (which would contain cookie attributes) is not configured with `SameSite` or `Secure` options anywhere in the codebase. The Tornado settings in `lib/streamlit/web/server/server.py` only define the cookie name (`"xsrf_cookie_name": "_streamlit_xsrf"`) without additional cookie attributes. To fix this, the server would need to configure `xsrf_cookie_kwargs` with appropriate `SameSite` and `Secure` values, potentially as configurable options.

### Related Issues

- **#9397** - [Axios 403 error with file uploader when site is embedded in Iframe](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/9397) — Very closely related; reports the same 403 error with `st.file_uploader` in iframes, with explicit mention that the `_streamlit_xsrf` cookie is missing the `SameSite` attribute.

- **#9719** - [BUG: Unable to upload files due to both AxiosError (Network and 403)](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/9719) — Similar symptoms with file uploads failing in Kubernetes deployments, likely caused by the same underlying CORS/XSRF cookie configuration issues.

- **#2517** - [Streamlit removes _xsrf cookie even with 'server.enableXsrfProtection=False'](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/2517) — Related issue that discusses the same `SameSite`/`Secure` cookie problem (see [comment #1321281460](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/2517#issuecomment-1321281460) which provides detailed analysis and potential fixes).

title: Misconfigured _xsrf cookies
text:
[NONE] I'm using a proprietary webapp based gui (no clue if built on electron, vscode, or what), and packaged an extension for it wrapping a streamlit app in an iframe.
File uploaded was broken with AxiosError 403, and I was able to narrow the problem down to the xsrf cookie being invalidly treated. (Ex, in normal conditions, deleting the cookie and uploading a file would also cause this error).

Patching streamlit per the #7358 PR (setting the `_streamlit_xsrf` cookie to Same-Site: None , Secure = True/Set ) fixed this issue.
https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Set-Cookie

I believe per MDN docs "Some browsers use Lax as the default value if SameSite is not specified", which are chromium based browsers; FF and safari don't do this.
So, for us, the problem was "browser"-specific: whatever this "browser" is setting it to by default breaks validation.
FWIW, applying the above patch fixed it in this "browser" and didn't break chromium based browsers.

I'd look forward to this issue getting resolved, or an equivalent patch being made known, during the starlette migration.

title: Optimize Streamlit core static files and library imports to reduce app startup time
text:
Issue #5798: Optimize Streamlit core static files and library imports to reduce app startup time
Labels: type:enhancement, area:performance

### Problem

Streamlit apps always take a few moments to load. One reason for this is the amount and size of the several static files that need to be fetched; another, the libraries that need to be imported in the .py files.

### Solution

A combination of the following:
- Reduce amount of files in `streamlit/static/static` that are fetched with GET requests.
- Reduce size of files in `streamlit/static/static` that are fetched with GET requests.
- Lazy loading of static files (for example, currently the files in `streamlit/static/vendor` are always loaded in `streamlit/static/index.html`, even though not all apps might use bokeh and graphviz widgets).
- Lazy loading of libraries imported in the .py files.

text: [NONE] Hi [USER], Personally I've been aware of this for a long time and while I understand that this is a design decision, I have never understood the rationale for this particular choice. One reason why I do not like it is that passing `key` to the widget is an explicit attempt to save the widget state in the session state. It is a very convenient syntactic sugar for associating widgets with explicit updates to `st.session_state` - or it would be, except it does not actually do that and it's not very upfront about that fact. Personally, if the widget has been declared with the `key`, it usually means that I want to keep the state independently of whether the widget is currently displayed or not. Sometimes I do not care. And although I can certainly imagine valid reasons why someone would want the state to go away with the widget, I have never wanted it to, and if I did, I would prefer to explicitly clear the state anyway. The fact that the saving is conditional on the widget being there and that fact is not very explicitly sign-posted in the description of the `key` parameter is very confusing to newcomers. I do not think it is much of an overstatement to say that on https://discuss.streamlit.io/ there is a thread about "why am I losing my widget state?" every other day. For those of us who do know about it it results in code littered with callback functions which

title: Preserve widget state when a widget disappears from the page (demoed via Multipage Apps)
text: an overstatement to say that on https://discuss.streamlit.io/ there is a thread about "why am I losing my widget state?" every other day. For those of us who do know about it it results in code littered with callback functions which serve only the purpose of running the 'fake' widget session state into the 'real' persistent widget state. I think the bottom line with this is that the way Streamlit state works now, there are three modes: 1. transient (normal widgets) 2. persistent (`st.session_state`) 3. persistent, but only sometimes (widget session state) The existence of the third one is, in my opinion, not very useful. Objectively, it is poorly documented. The [Session State API reference](https://docs.streamlit.io/library/api-reference/session-state) treats the two like as if they were the same thing: >Every widget with a key is automatically added to Session State: The [Multipage Apps](https://docs.streamlit.io/library/get-started/multipage-apps) site explicitly says: >Pages share the same [st.session_state](https://docs.streamlit.io/library/advanced-features/session-state): The linked page says: >Session State provides the functionality to store variables across reruns. The only place that does is the [Advanced notes on widget behaviour](https://docs.streamlit.io/library/advanced-features/widget-semantics): >If you don't call a widget function in a script run, we neither store the widget state nor render the widget. If you call a widget function with the same arguments later, Streamlit treats it as a new widget. While updating the documentation to really drive home the real behavior could be one solution, I would argue that whoever wrote the documentation described how this process would work in an intuitive manner: *if you put the `key` on a widget, the state will be saved in `st.session.state`, which persists between pages*, and it's the real behavior that is counter-intuitive.

title: Preserve widget state when a widget disappears from the page (demoed via Multipage Apps)
text:
[CONTRIBUTOR] Hey [USER] 

As of today, this is _expected behavior_, but I understand why this is confusing. We have adopted the mechanism that widgets that disappear from the page are removed from session state. There was a lot of confusion on what this means. The counter-bug we received is saying "Why does the widget continue to have a value after it disappeared?"

MPA demonstrates this problem by switching pages effectively removes widgets from session_state. There are two ways to think about the UX.

1.  MPA are "separate" apps. In this case, values set by session state are preserved, but values set by widget state (in session state) will disappear in the next run after the widget is removed. The idea is that each page is it's own self-functioning app, and therefore we expect the widget state to reset when going back to it.
2. MPA session state is all shared including widget state. This is what you are advocating as the expected behavior.

In the end, we identified (1) as the model to use and agreed on. I think the main reasoning is that to achieve (2) behavior, you simply save your widget state into session state as a separate variable. It's a little clunky though. I will leave this issue open to get feedback and ideas from the community.

Adds a keyword-only `persist_state=None | "page" | "session"` parameter to most widgets that preserves a keyed widget's value when it stops being rendered. Persistence is purely a server-side state decision.

- `None` (default): current behavior — value is lost when the widget isn't rendered or on a page switch.
- `"page"`: keep the value while the widget isn't rendered on the **same page**; drop it on a page switch (not restored on return, and never leaks to another page that reuses the key).
- `"session"`: keep the value for the whole session, including across page switches.

[COLLABORATOR] ## Update 

I wrote a spec for this recently: https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/14787, and we started implementing this for our widgets: https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/14828

[COLLABORATOR] Starting with Streamlit 1.66, all relevant widgets support `on_change="ignore"`. The widget updates in the browser without triggering a rerun, and Python receives the new value on the next rerun triggered by another interaction, such as a button click.

This also lets you build dynamic forms that `st.form` can't express, since some inputs can still rerun to update others:

```python
import streamlit as st

CITIES = {"Germany": ["Berlin", "Munich"], "France": ["Paris", "Lyon"]}

country = st.selectbox("Country", list(CITIES))  # Reruns to refresh the city options
city = st.selectbox("City", CITIES[country], on_change="ignore")
name = st.text_input("Name", on_change="ignore")

if st.button("Save"):
    st.write(f"Saved {name} from {city}, {country}")
```

Since ignored values only reach Python on the next rerun, use it for inputs where users don't expect an immediate reaction.

title: Provide methods to refresh caching
text:
Issue #5871: Provide methods to refresh caching
Labels: type:enhancement, feature:cache

### Problem

Parts of my dashboard require sourcing CSV files from external hosts, and it can take a long time (60s) to download and processes that data. However, the data is made available at 6am every day. I already have a function which uses streamlit cache around my data fetching, but it would be amazing if I could say "at 6:05am every day, call this function".

### Solution

**MVP:** Streamlit should have a decorator you can apply to functions so they run at startup. These functions could make use of existing python scheduling libraries like apscheduler to call (and thus refresh) caching whenever needed.

**Possible additions:** Streamlit could extend its decorators, integrating the scheduling side through decorator parameters and abstracting that away from the user.

### Additional context

FR raised from this forum post: https://discuss.streamlit.io/t/eagerly-execute-specific-functions-on-app-launch/34957

It seems a few people have been trying to figure out how to refresh caching, and it would be good to not have to use selenium to simulate a web request from an external service to do so.

text:
[COLLABORATOR] ## Update

Streamlit 1.61 will support a `refresh_mode="background"` for `cache_data` and `cache_resource` which allows expired values (based on `ttl`) to be updated in the background without blocking the user session.

[NONE] Thanks for working on this. If I understand the spec correctly, this will essentially extend the caching to 2 x TTL, where a background refresh will get triggered between 1x <-> 2x TTL.  Beyond 2x TTL it's existing blocking cache refresh behavior.

So this will solve some subset of use cases, but will not help for infrequently accessed slow functions (where typical time between usage is longer than the tolerable data staleness/TTL).

The PR and spec discuss the potential unbound memory/resource problem that comes with solutions that would proactively refresh the cache before TTL expiration (unbound combinations of cached function parameters).  And some complexity of needing a background scheduler thread of some sort. However, it would be good for a future implementation to include this, with the user making the choice knowingly (and potentially with a max entry upper bound).

I sometime use the pattern where my cached slow function is only ever executed with one set of parameters, returning potentially more data to some calling function than necessary, and let that calling function do further filtering.  This calling function is not cached and has the  unbound arbitrary user supplied parameters.  This was I get more cache hits at the expense of a bit more filtering compute.

That pattern would benefit greatly from an "eager"/"proactive" cache refresher that executes before TTL expiration.

title: Provide methods to refresh caching
text:
[COLLABORATOR] [USER] thanks, great feedback! We have been thinking about this aspect quite a bit when designing the background refresh mode. The current solution is a bit of a balance to have a simple API with minimal risk for users of blowing up memory and compute. 

But the good news is that it is already possible to implement a scheduled background refresh via `lifespan` in `st.App`, e.g.:

```python
# data.py
import streamlit as st

[USER].cache_data(ttl="1h", refresh_mode="background")
def load_data(dataset: str):
    return fetch_expensive_data(dataset)
```

```python
# app.py
from collections.abc import AsyncIterator
from contextlib import asynccontextmanager
import logging

import anyio
import streamlit as st

from data import load_data

_LOGGER = logging.getLogger(__name__)


async def keep_cache_warm() -> None:
    while True:
        try:
            # Cheap while fresh. Once stale, this returns the stale value and
            # triggers Streamlit's deduplicated background refresh.
            await anyio.to_thread.run_sync(load_data, "dashboard")
        except Exception:
            _LOGGER.exception("Scheduled cache refresh failed")

        await anyio.sleep(60)  # Check freshness every minute


[USER]
async def lifespan(_app: st.App) -> AsyncIterator[None]:
    async with anyio.create_task_group() as task_group:
        task_group.start_soon(keep_cache_warm)
        try:
            yield
        finally:
            task_group.cancel_scope.cancel()


app = st.App("dashboard.py", lifespan=lifespan)
```

And we are planning to make this even simpler with a native utility command to define background tasks (related request: https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/6687).

title: Button or API for users to switch between themes
text:
[NONE] Here is the solution provided by [Cursor](https://www.cursor.com/) :)

It involves putting a file `themes.toml` in `.streamlit` folder which has all the themes you want to select from.

```
# Load themes from themes.toml
def load_themes():
    themes_file = os.path.join('.streamlit', 'themes.toml')
    if os.path.exists(themes_file):
        with open(themes_file, 'r') as f:
            themes = toml.load(f)
            return {k.replace('theme.', ''): v for k, v in themes.items()}
    return {}

# Update theme function
def update_theme(theme_dict):
    for key, value in theme_dict.items():
        st._config.set_option(f"theme.{key}", value)  # type: ignore # noqa: SLF001


# Theme selector
themes = load_themes()
theme_names = list(themes.keys())
selected_theme = st.sidebar.selectbox(
    "Select Theme",
    theme_names,
    index=theme_names.index('dark') if 'dark' in theme_names else 0
)

# Apply theme if changed
if 'current_theme' not in st.session_state:
    st.session_state.current_theme = selected_theme

if selected_theme != st.session_state.current_theme:
    update_theme(themes[selected_theme])
    st.session_state.current_theme = selected_theme
    st.rerun()
```

title: Persist widget state if `key` is set, even if the widget is not rendered
text:
Issue #6074: Persist widget state if `key` is set, even if the widget is not rendered
Labels: type:enhancement, area:widgets, feature:st.session_state

👋 I work on developer experience for Streamlit and wanted to get some feedback on this recurring issue.

**TL;DR: Take a look at the [example app](https://keyed-widget-state-issue.streamlit.app/) and let us know how it impacts you, and what you think about how to fix this issue!**

**Discussion on the forums [here](https://discuss.streamlit.io/t/keyed-widget-state-persistence-discussion-possible-fixes/37359)**

One of the current Streamlit behaviors that causes confusion for many of us is how widgets with `key='foo'` lose their session_state value when they are not rendered in a given run. It seems to come up most often with multipage apps that have some state dependency between pages, but also possible in a single page app with conditional rendering. A minimal example:

```
view = st.radio("View", ["view1", "view2"])

if view == "view1":
    st.text_input("Text1", key="text1")
    "☝️ Enter some text, then click on view2 above"
elif view == "view2":
    "☝️ Now go back to view1 and see if your text is still there"
```

I'm working with [USER] on whether / how to update this behavior so it's more intuitive, or at least possible to get the intuitive behavior easily.

I put together a simple example app showing the behavior and linking some of the prior issues about it:
[https://keyed-widget-state-issue.streamlit.app/](https://keyed-widget-state-issue.streamlit.app/)

### Questions

title: Persist widget state if `key` is set, even if the widget is not rendered
text:
I put together a simple example app showing the behavior and linking some of the prior issues about it:
[https://keyed-widget-state-issue.streamlit.app/](https://keyed-widget-state-issue.streamlit.app/)

### Questions

- Do you have a full working public app where you had to hack around this (such as duplicating or using "shadow keys")? Please share with us!
- Do you have an app or use case where you rely on the current behavior (widget has `key` set but needs value to reset after not rendering), that will break if we change this? We **really** want to hear about these! Please share!

### Possible fixes

It seems like most developers we hear from find the current behavior very unintuitive, and we see a lot more use cases that have to work around this rather than benefit from it.
- Given that, should we just do a breaking change to the default behavior to persist, like most of us seem to expect?
- If so: We should still provide a path to clear keyed widget state when needed. Need to figure out how to best do this.

If not a breaking change: most proposals seem to prefer something like a `persist=` key. For example, both [USER] and [USER] propose something like this in [#4458](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/4458). Thoughts on this approach, or other ideas?

title: Persist widget state if `key` is set, even if the widget is not rendered
text: [NONE] Thanks for throwing shade at this issue! I've built a really complex app with streamlit, and have been stung time and again due to this behaviour. See for e.g. - https://gooey.ai/video-bots/ --- Currently using the following workaround for this - 1. Don't use keys. Instead, store the initial value inside the session state, and update the state manually. 2. If the widget goes out of view, make sure the initial values are up to date ```python from time import sleep from streamlit.runtime.state import get_session_state import streamlit as st init_key = "__init_values__" def main(): view = st.radio("View", ["view1", "view2"]) if view == "view1": text_input("Text1", key="text1") "☝️ Enter some text, then click on view2 above" elif view == "view2": "☝️ Now go back to view1 and see if your text is still there" st.write(st.session_state) def text_input(label, key): if init_key not in st.session_state: st.session_state[init_key] = {} initial_values = st.session_state[init_key] try: value = initial_values[key] except KeyError: value = st.session_state.get(key, "") initial_values[key] = value value = st.text_input(label, value=value) st.session_state[key] = value return value def ensure_hidden_widgets_loaded(): new_session_state = get_session_state()._state._new_session_state for key, value in st.session_state.items(): if key in new_session_state or key == init_key: continue st.session_state[init_key][key] = value try: main() finally: ensure_hidden_widgets_loaded() ``` --- IMO the idea of keys, in general, needs to be rethought. They cause really hard-to-debug issues. E.g. see how the `slider` widget behaves when provided with a key. And also how text editing is jumpy when a piece of blocking code is executed. But permanently changing this behaviour would be an excellent start.

title: Persist widget state if `key` is set, even if the widget is not rendered
text:
[NONE] > One of the current Streamlit behaviors that causes confusion for many of us is how widgets with `key='foo'` lose their session_state value when they are not rendered in a given run

Well in fact their widget state [gets deleted](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/ef8bb02b27ab26780c07814ee77d4c5e91de62c7/lib/streamlit/runtime/state/session_state.py#L599-L608) while session state is persisted across re-runs.
Given how this distinction is already [exposed](https://docs.streamlit.io/library/advanced-features/session-state#session-state-and-widget-state-association), it could make be left to users to decide whether or not to preserve widget state across reruns.
Given that this tends to affect more complicated apps, I would presume we mostly wouldn't even mind a component-level`persist_state=True` flag. An app-wide setting would be an improvement without polluting the API.

As a catch with app-wide behavior, conditionally rendered widgets can have different valid options/number ranges when being rendered again, possibly making the persisted state now invalid.

[CONTRIBUTOR] > As a catch with app-wide behavior, conditionally rendered widgets can have different valid options/number ranges when being rendered again, possibly making the persisted state now invalid.

Yes, if the widget arguments change, we will always re-create the widget and clear any prior values/state. I don't think there's any consideration to change that behavior, since as you said it can lead to invalid states pretty easily.

[NONE] 👍

Great to read this thread. Although I really like Streamlit this behaviour makes it pretty much impossible to use it when working with a lot of filter settings. A ‘persist=‘ flag would work, but I prefer it with True as default.

title: Persist widget state if `key` is set, even if the widget is not rendered
text: [CONTRIBUTOR] My organization has over 20 multipage Streamlit apps, and none of them find the current default useful, so I'm definitely in favour of a breaking change here. I'm currently going through an exercise where I'm building a Streamlit proxy object which does the following: * Intercept all calls to streamlit, and if the attribute is a callable, set the item in session_state using the same default logic that the widget would normally apply. For example, set multiselect box default to `[]` rather than `None` * Pop value/default/index from args * Wrap the callable with a function that sets the state item in our own state dictionary, only if the widget has a key defined and allows writing Here's the bulk of the code: ``` def __getattr__(self, name): attr = getattr(self._original_st, name) if callable(attr): # If the attribute is a function/method, wrap it def persist_widget_values(*args, **kwargs): logging.info( f"Intercepted call to {name} with args={args}, kwargs={kwargs}" ) # If a key exists, persist it! key = kwargs.get("key", None) if key: # This lets us handle cases where widgets are called with only # positional arguments, eg: st.radio("radio1", ["option1", "option2"]) # so we can correctly infer defaults all_args_as_kwargs = inspect.getcallargs(attr, *args, **kwargs) logging.debug(f"Re-wrote arguments to {all_args_as_kwargs}") self._set_default_value(name, key, all_args_as_kwargs) # We have to always pop the default/value setting kwargs to avoid WidgetStateDuplicationWarning for k in ["value", "default", "index"]: kwargs.pop(k, None) if name not in UNCONTROLLABLE_WIDGETS: # List of widgets with writes_allowed = False value = self._original_st.session_state[key] self.items_to_persist[key] = value logging.info(f"Interrupting cleanup for {key}")

title: Persist widget state if `key` is set, even if the widget is not rendered
text: always pop the default/value setting kwargs to avoid WidgetStateDuplicationWarning for k in ["value", "default", "index"]: kwargs.pop(k, None) if name not in UNCONTROLLABLE_WIDGETS: # List of widgets with writes_allowed = False value = self._original_st.session_state[key] self.items_to_persist[key] = value logging.info(f"Interrupting cleanup for {key}") self._original_st.session_state[key] = value return attr( *args, **kwargs ) # Call the function with our updated kwargs return persist_widget_values ``` * Each time a page is initialized, restore state items which have been cleaned up: ``` def restore_persisted_items(self): """Restores state items which were linked to Streamlit widgets that are no longer displayed on the page. This allows us to keep tracking state items even if the current page doesn't use widgets with those keys """ for key, value in self.items_to_persist.items(): if key not in self._original_st.session_state: self._original_st.session_state[key] = value ```

title: Schedule clear cache
text:
Issue #6625: Schedule clear cache
Labels: type:enhancement, feature:cache, feature:community-cloud

### Problem

I learned that the cache from "st.cache_data()" will only be cleared when the option "Clear cache" from developer options is manually activated by the owner of the app or if the cache expires. 

The problem with that is when you have multiple sets of data in your app that are scheduled to be updated in specific dates of the month, at specific times, you either go and manually clear cache yourself in each of this updates or you'll have outdated data in your app until the cache expires.
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/73763541/236198590-0ef4604e-1c36-4379-89d4-2663704f5ddc.png)

Of course you can leave a small time for the argument "ttl" in "st.cache_data()" to try to get around this issue but you will be querying your database multiple times, and also increasing user loading time, when you know the data hasn't changed (in my case, the data is only updated once a month). This also creates the issue that the user of the app won't have the most recent data as soon as it is released.

### Solution

It would be great to be able to leave a really long time as an argument to "st.cache_data()" and be able to schedule a "Clear cache" on the app settings (https://share.streamlit.io/) for when you know the data is gonna be released along the following months.

title: Non-script blocking functions for long-running tasks (background execution)
text:
Issue #6687: Non-script blocking functions for long-running tasks (background execution)
Labels: type:enhancement, feature:cache, area:performance, type:possible-component, area:threading/processing

### Problem

Many applications require long-running functions. In many cases, `[USER].cache_data` and `[USER].cache_resource` will suffice to achieve good performance, but these are not suitable when the inputs to the function change very frequently. 

One common sub-case of this is where the output of the function is important, but not time critical. In this case it would be good to render the page and then "fill-in" the missing parts when the function finishes running.

### Solution

**MVP:** What's the smallest possible solution that would get 80% of the problem out of the way?

I propose a decorator `st.run_in_background` that returns a spinner (like the `st.cache_resource` decorator) while a function is running, but does not block the execution of the application. 

To illustrate the idea:

```python
[USER].run_in_background(show_spinner='Generating the plot')
def plot_data(data):
    '''Just an example of a slow function'''
    return sns.pairplot(data)

def get_results(data):
    '''Just an example of a fast function'''
    return 'All good' 

st.title('My app')

selected_data = ... # let's assume this changes a lot, eg. due to interactive filters
results = get_results(selected_data)

fig = plot_data(selected_data ) # This is slow to run
st.pyplot(fig)

st.write(results)
```

In the code above, it'd be great if `st.pyplot` displayed a spinner while `plot_data` is executing (without blocking `st.write(results)`) and then "fill-in" the space with the plot once `plot_data` finishes executing.

**Possible additions:** What are other things that could be added to the MVP over time to make it better?

title: Non-script blocking functions for long-running tasks (background execution)
text:
**Possible additions:** What are other things that could be added to the MVP over time to make it better?

fig = plot_data(data)
fig.update_axes(...) # this would error if fig is not a matplotlib figure, it'd be awesome if streamlit could figure out this is still being loaded without blocking execution
```

Ultimately I'm proposing that streamlit replicate the lazy loading as done in PowerBI (for example)

![image](https://apps.provingground.io/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2020/08/Tracer-OfficeSpaceDash.gif)

title: Non-script blocking functions for long-running tasks (background execution)
text:
[NONE] If there'd be a way to report progress (not just spinner) for such task too - would be awesome.

[CONTRIBUTOR] Hey all — this issue has been on my radar and I wanted to share some design thinking. Sharing it here since this issue already captures the problem well and I'd love to get reactions.

### The idea: `st.background_task`

A managed API for kicking off long-running work that survives reruns:

```python
task = st.background_task(slow_query, args=(params,), key="my_query")

if task.running:
    st.info("Query running...")
elif task.done:
    st.dataframe(task.result)
```

The `key` deduplicates across reruns (same key = same task, not a new one). When the task finishes, the runtime automatically triggers a rerun so you can render the result — no polling needed. Tasks get cleaned up when the session ends.

The workaround [USER] shared above with raw threads works, but threads created outside Streamlit don't have access to `ScriptRunContext`, can't trigger reruns on completion, and aren't tied to the session lifecycle. This would handle all of that.

### How it relates to parallel fragments

We're working on `[USER].fragment(parallel=True)` ([#14277](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/14277)) which gives concurrency *within* a single script run — independent UI sections load at the same time. Background tasks would be different: the work outlives reruns, produces data rather than UI, and doesn't block interactions. They'd be complementary.

### Open questions

- Does the API shape feel right? The original proposal here used a decorator (`[USER].run_in_background`) — any preference?
- What are your actual use cases? Long queries, model training, batch jobs?
- How important is cancellation when inputs change?

Would love to hear what people think.

title: Non-script blocking functions for long-running tasks (background execution)
text:
[CONTRIBUTOR] An update here: now that we have the features of `st.cache_data(refresh_mode="background")` and `st.fragment(parallel=True)` there is a pattern for this combining these. 

See the app that I have created here illustrating how to use these for long-running tasks: https://long-query-patterns.streamlit.app/
See also this PR updating our skills: https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/17446

Note, there is a gap associated with this that has surfaced while testing this pattern, when you have a user interaction with an element that is inside a fragment, that will not interrupt the main run and will need to wait for the long running task to complete. I created an issue to track this here: https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/17445 . If this is affecting your use case, please upvote and comment on that issue. Please let me know if you have any other use cases which this suggested pattern does not address 🙏

title: Bad message format error when using containers
text: [CONTRIBUTOR] This is a bug involving the interaction between `st.container` and `st.session_state`. The issue occurs when a container is stored in session state and reused to create widgets dynamically. The root cause appears to be a **delta path synchronization issue**: when a container is stored in `st.session_state`, its cursor and delta path are captured at that moment. When the container is reused in subsequent script runs, the delta path becomes stale because the frontend's element tree structure has changed. This causes the "Bad 'setIn' index X (should be between [0, Y])" error in `SetNodeByDeltaPathVisitor.ts` when attempting to set elements at invalid indices. The error is surfaced as "Bad message format" in the UI via the error handler in `App.tsx`. ### Related Issues - **#5402** - ["Bad 'setIn' index XX" when using st.cache_data in thread](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/5402) - **Highly related**. Same underlying frontend error ("Bad 'setIn' index") occurring in a different context (threaded caching with spinners). Both issues suggest problems with delta path synchronization when elements are created outside the normal script flow. - **#12762** - [Key is ignored when using fragments and containers](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/12762) - Related. This involves containers with fragments where widget keys don't behave correctly, leading to duplicate elements. Similar pattern of container + dynamic content issues. - **#5044** - [empty() does not remove cleared elements](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/5044) - Related. Another container state management bug where `st.empty()` doesn't properly clean up internal widget state, leading to synchronization issues between the frontend and backend element trees. --- *This is an automated triage comment. title: Is it possible to make Streamlit interactive plot as fast as Plotly?
text:
Issue #6978: Is it possible to make Streamlit interactive plot as fast as Plotly?
Labels: type:enhancement, feature:st.plotly_chart

### Problem

[![Open in Streamlit Cloud](https://static.streamlit.io/badges/streamlit_badge_black_white.svg)](https://issues.streamlitapp.com/?issue=gh-6978)

I am trying to create a responsive plot in Streamlit that responds to a slider bar, but it is extremely slow.

```
import numpy as np
import plotly.graph_objects as go
import streamlit as st


if st.session_state.get('fig') is None:
    st.session_state['freq'] = np.arange(0.0, 5.1, 0.1).round(2)    
    f = st.session_state['freq'][2]
    st.session_state['fig'] = go.Figure()
    st.session_state['fig'].add_trace(
        go.Scatter(
            name=str(f),
            x=np.arange(0, 10.01, 0.01),
            y=np.sin(f* np.arange(0, 10.01, 0.01))))
    
def sldier_callback():
    f = st.session_state['slider_freq']
    x = st.session_state['fig'].data[0].x
    st.session_state['fig'].data[0].y = np.sin(f*x)
    st.session_state['fig'].data[0].name = str(f)


f = st.select_slider(
    label='Frequency', 
    options=st.session_state['freq'],
    value=2,
    on_change=sldier_callback,
    key='slider_freq'
)

st.plotly_chart(st.session_state['fig'])
```

![image](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/assets/15989924/de4641d3-ee8b-44f3-9893-81f58d371e17)

### Solution

The [Plotly chart](https://plotly.com/python/sliders/), on the other hand, is much more responsive to the slider bar. It creates and hides the figures at the beginning and then unhides the correct figure when you move the slider bar.

```
import plotly.graph_objects as go
import numpy as np


fig = go.Figure()
for step in np.arange(0, 5, 0.1):
    fig.add_trace(
        go.Scatter(
            visible=False,
            name="f = " + str(step),
            x=np.arange(0, 10, 0.01),
            y=np.sin(step * np.arange(0, 10, 0.01))))

fig.data[10].visible = True

# Create and add slider
steps = []
for i in range(len(fig.data)):
    step = dict(
        method="update",
        args=[              
            {"visible": [False] * len(fig.data)},
            {"title": "Slider switched to step: " + str(i)}],  
    )
    step["args"][0]["visible"][i] = True
    steps.append(step)

sliders = [dict(
    active=10,
    currentvalue={"prefix": "Frequency: "},
    pad={"t": 50},
    steps=steps
)]

fig.update_layout(
    sliders=sliders
)

fig.show()
```

![image](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/assets/15989924/b1c3b597-9a86-403f-8e6b-8ce9bfe3e0dc)

### Additional context

text:

### Additional context

I tried to do the same in Streamlit with the following code, but it is still very slow. Does anyone know how to speed it up in Streamlit? Thanks!

```
import streamlit as st
import numpy as np
import plotly.graph_objects as go


if st.session_state.get('fig') is None:
    st.session_state['freq'] = np.arange(0.0, 5.01, 0.1).round(2)
    st.session_state['fig'] = go.Figure()

    st.session_state['selected'] = 0
    st.session_state['fig'].data[0].visible = True


def sldier_callback():
    i = st.session_state['selected']
    st.session_state['fig'].data[i].visible = False
    freq = st.session_state['slider_freq']
    i = np.where(st.session_state['freq']==freq)[0][0]
    st.session_state['fig'].data[i].visible = True
    st.session_state['selected'] = i


f = st.select_slider(
    label='freq', 
    options=st.session_state['freq'],
    value=2,
    on_change=sldier_callback,
    key='slider_freq'
)

st.plotly_chart(st.session_state['fig'])
```

title: Is it possible to make Streamlit interactive plot as fast as Plotly?
text:
[COLLABORATOR] [USER] Thanks for the enhancement request. I was able to reproduce this [here](https://issues.streamlitapp.com/?issue=gh-6978). Two important pieces of information on this: 
1. using `st.slider` will always be slower than the approach that directly combines it with a plotly slider since the `st.slider` approach requires a roundtrip from frontend -> backend -> frontend, while the Plotly slider only works on the frontend. 
2. You can just use the plotly slider also on a Streamlit frontend with the same speed, e.g.:

```python
import streamlit as st
import plotly.graph_objects as go
import numpy as np


fig = go.Figure()
for step in np.arange(0, 5, 0.1):
    fig.add_trace(
        go.Scatter(
            visible=False,
            name="f = " + str(step),
            x=np.arange(0, 10, 0.01),
            y=np.sin(step * np.arange(0, 10, 0.01))))

fig.data[10].visible = True

# Create and add slider
steps = []
for i in range(len(fig.data)):
    step = dict(
        method="update",
        args=[              
            {"visible": [False] * len(fig.data)},
            {"title": "Slider switched to step: " + str(i)}],  
    )
    step["args"][0]["visible"][i] = True
    steps.append(step)

sliders = [dict(
    active=10,
    currentvalue={"prefix": "Frequency: "},
    pad={"t": 50},
    steps=steps
)]

fig.update_layout(
    sliders=sliders
)

st.plotly_chart(fig)
```

title: Is it possible to make Streamlit interactive plot as fast as Plotly?
text: [COLLABORATOR] Closing this since we provide `st.fragment` that allows to group widgets with charts or other elements to provide very fast interactions between those. This will still not be as fast as native plotly widgets since it still requires a roundtrip to our server.

[COLLABORATOR] [USER] `st.data_editor` probably yes. But won't be added for `st.table`. 

[COLLABORATOR] ## Update

This will be possible via the `st.column_config.ButtonColumn` in Streamlit 1.59+.

The values in the configured column become the button labels, and when a button is clicked Streamlit stores a one-shot click payload in `st.session_state[key]` with the clicked `row` and `label`.

For example:

```python
import pandas as pd
import streamlit as st

df = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "name": ["Alice", "Bob", "Charlie"],
        "action": [":material/visibility: View"] * 3,
    }
)


def handle_view():
    click = st.session_state.view_click
    row = df.iloc[click["row"]]
    st.toast(f"Viewing {row['name']}")


st.dataframe(
    df,
    column_config={
        "action": st.column_config.ButtonColumn(
            "Action",
            type="tertiary",
            on_click=handle_view,
            key="view_click",
        )
    },
    hide_index=True,
)
```

You can also provide multiple actions per row by using a list of labels in the cell value:

```python
df = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "name": ["Alice", "Bob", "Charlie"],
        "actions": [
            [":material/edit: Edit", ":material/delete: Delete"],
            [":material/edit: Edit", ":material/delete: Delete"],
            [":material/edit: Edit"],
        ],
    }
)


def handle_action():
    click = st.session_state.action_click
    row = df.iloc[click["row"]]

    if "Delete" in click["label"]:
        st.warning(f"Deleting {row['name']}")
    elif "Edit" in click["label"]:
        st.info(f"Editing {row['name']}")


st.dataframe(
    df,
    column_config={
        "actions": st.column_config.ButtonColumn(
            "Actions",
            on_click=handle_action,
            key="action_click",
        )
    },
    hide_index=True,
)
```

`ButtonColumn` also works in `st.data_editor`; the button cells are read-only, but clicks still trigger the callback.

title: UI jitters, chart flashes for minutes when a complex Altair chart is used in multipage app (Chrome)
text:
Issue #7041: UI jitters, chart flashes for minutes when a complex Altair chart is used in multipage app (Chrome)
Labels: type:bug, priority:P3, feature:st.altair_chart

### Checklist

- [X] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar issues.
- [X] I added a very descriptive title to this issue.
- [X] I have provided sufficient information below to help reproduce this issue.

### Summary

The Streamlit UI "jitters"  when a complex Altair chart is used in a multi-page app  in `st.altair_chart`. 

What I mean by "jitter" is best seen in the attached video.

* The jitter can last for tens of seconds and even minutes and renders the app unusable. Eventually it stops most of the times, but not always.
* The chart sometimes flashes during the jitter.
* It occurs with charts bigger **and** smaller than the screen width.
* ~~Setting  `use_container_width=True` reduces the jitter to a half second or so, such that the app becomes usable, but it is noticeable.~~ This is not consistent. I've also seen it with  `use_container_width=True` now.

### Summary

The selectbox UI could be clearer to users.  In our use case editing the selectbox makes no sense.   The arrow key interactions were difficult because the selected row would go off-screen rather than autoscrolling to keep the selected item in view.  When arrowing around, the UI was expected to update rather than require the enter key.

### Reproducible Code Example

[![Open in Streamlit Cloud](https://static.streamlit.io/badges/streamlit_badge_black_white.svg)](https://issues.streamlitapp.com/?issue=gh-7187)

```Python
import streamlit as st


selection = st.selectbox("My List Box", [ f'Option {i}' for i in range(1,100) ] )
```

### Steps To Reproduce

Run the program, edit the text in select box, and then arrow around in the selectbox until the highlighted line disappears off the top or bottom of the listbox.

### Expected Behavior

I expect select boxes to at least optionally be read-only (my 90% default is read-only)
I expect select boxes to have more than one item visible. Optionally, depending on screen space, I'm fine specifying the height in pixels or items.
I expect select boxes to keep the selected item visible under all conditions while using arrow keys.
I would like to optionally be able to control whether arrowing in the list box triggers a change in the UI

### Current Behavior

title: st.selectbox user experience is confusing.
text:
### Current Behavior

I watched users interact with the selectbox UI I made for them and was shocked by their confusion.

title: st.selectbox user experience is confusing.
text:
### Current Behavior

I watched users interact with the selectbox UI I made for them and was shocked by their confusion.

1) Several users immediately started EDITING the text, which confused me as I watched!  This is the very last thing I expected a selectbox to allow. It never occurred to me to type.  My use case is selecting options, not free-form text entry.  This became a pseudo-feature for longer lists, acting as a filter only showing items that matched the typed text (this could be very useful as some UI toolkits have this type of widget). A `read_only=True`  or `filter_mode=True` could be useful.
2) Part of the reason for these issues was that selectboxes show one item until you interact with them, so they look like a text boxes.  It would be nice to have a `visible_items` parameter to allow control of vertical space.  Having only one item visible obscures the fact that there could be more than one, though admittedly, the height of 1 is optimal for vertical space.
3) The arrow keys act oddly.  Users are used to arrowing up/down and having the selected item change, and when the selected item gets to the top or bottom, the UI should scroll to keep giving feedback on what is selected. In Steamlit, the highlighted item goes off-screen, breaking the UI feedback.
4) It would be nice if arrowing "triggered" a UI update to give immediate feedback.  I see the need for arrowing + enter key to trigger the change for use cases that are expensive in time.  An `auto_update=True` might be nice.

[COLLABORATOR] ## Update

`st.text_input` now supports client-side regex validation with a custom error message through the new `validate` parameter. This will be available in Streamlit `1.62+`.

```python
email = st.text_input(
    "Email",
    validate=(r"^[^@\s]+@[^@\s]+\.[^@\s]+$", "Enter a valid email address."),
)
```

Invalid non-empty values are not submitted, and the custom message is shown when validation fails.

title: Limiting maximum and minimum of st.date_input's selectable dates to the maximum/minimum of datetime.datetime
text:
Issue #7427: Limiting maximum and minimum of st.date_input's selectable dates to the maximum/minimum of datetime.datetime
Labels: type:enhancement, feature:st.date_input

### Checklist

- [X] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar feature requests.
- [X] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

Setting the maximum available value of Python's datetime as default for st.date_input causes issues.
The function internally tries to set a value 10 years later for the selection widget and then crashes.

To reproduce the behaviour, run this code: 

```
import streamlit as st
from datetime import datetime
st.date_input('Enter Timespan:', value=[datetime.today() , datetime.max])
```

The documentation for st.date_input includes a parameter to control the maximum value of the selection widget: 
> max_value : datetime.date or datetime.datetime
>     The maximum selectable date. If value is a date, defaults to value + 10 years.
>     If value is the interval [start, end], defaults to end + 10 years.

Setting the parameter max_value of st.date_input to datetime.max solves the issue.
`st.date_input('Enter Date:',  max_value=datetime.max, value=[datetime.today(), datetime.max])`

### Why?

This result is expected behaviour and can be inferred from the documentation. 
However, it seems rather inelegant/unintuitive to explicitly have to set an additional max_value when using the maximum value of the data type used.

### How?

Since date_input works with datetime internally, I'd set it to check datetime.max (and datetime.min, similarily) itself and not try to set its maximum to an impossible value.  
So to get the max selectable value in pseudocode would be:

title: Limiting maximum and minimum of st.date_input's selectable dates to the maximum/minimum of datetime.datetime
text:
### How?

Since date_input works with datetime internally, I'd set it to check datetime.max (and datetime.min, similarily) itself and not try to set its maximum to an impossible value.  
So to get the max selectable value in pseudocode would be:

```
max_value = max( value + 10 years, datetime.max)
```

If this behaviour is not desired, a nicer warning would be in order. 

```
Error message: 
ValueError: year 10009 is out of range
```

Took me a while to trace that back to streamlit internally adding 10 years. Maybe something like:

```
ValueError: Cannot set value 9999. Default value range for date_input [9989-10009] would be out of range for datetime. Please set max_value.
```

title: RuntimeError: There is no current event loop in thread error with Streamlit and Asyncio
text:
Issue #744: RuntimeError: There is no current event loop in thread error with Streamlit and Asyncio
Labels: type:enhancement, area:server, area:threading/processing

# Summary
I am running pyppeteer, which depends on asyncio, to load data which is only available in a rendered web page.  I experienced an error earlier with Jupyter, which depends on tornado, and where I received an error that `RuntimeError: This event loop is already running`. The reason is that tornado was reworked with asyncio and there didn't seem to be a realistic workaround by the Jupyter developers.  The issue was solved with this library [nest_asyncio](https://github.com/erdewit/nest_asyncio).  Whether I include nest_asyncio or not,  I receive the error `RuntimeError: There is no current event loop in thread 'ScriptRunner.scriptThread'`.

# Steps to reproduce
What are the steps we should take to reproduce the bug:

1. Initializing the RenderHTML class in the following imported file, will cause the error to be outputted as an error to the Streamlit UI.

```
import asyncio
import nest_asyncio
#nest_asyncio.apply()
from pyppeteer import launch

class HTMLMissing(Exception):
    '''An exception for a missing or invalid HTML.'''
    pass

class RenderHTML():

    def __init__(self, html=None):
        self.html = ""
        self.set_html(html)
        asyncio.get_event_loop().run_until_complete(self.build_page())

    async def build_page(self):
        browser = await launch()
        context = await browser.createIncognitoBrowserContext()
        self.page = await browser.newPage()

   ...other functions...
```

Load RenderHTML class, launch chrome, and build a new browser page.

![Views](https://api.views-badge.org/badge/st-issue-744)

[CONTRIBUTOR] This is a confirmed bug related to Streamlit's execution model and asyncio event loop handling. The root cause is that Streamlit's `ScriptRunner` creates a dedicated thread (`ScriptRunner.scriptThread`) to execute user scripts, but this thread does not have an asyncio event loop associated with it. When Python code calls `asyncio.get_event_loop()` from a thread without a running event loop (especially in Python 3.10+), it raises `RuntimeError: There is no current event loop in thread`. This affects any library that depends on asyncio (like pyppeteer, playwright, aiohttp, etc.).

The workaround is to manually create a new event loop in the script thread using `asyncio.new_event_loop()` and `asyncio.set_event_loop()`, but a proper fix would require Streamlit to either set up an event loop for the ScriptRunner thread or provide native async/await support.

### Related Issues

- **#8488** - [Native asyncio support](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/8488): This is the most directly related enhancement request. It proposes first-class async/await support in Streamlit, which would fundamentally address this issue by properly integrating asyncio into Streamlit's execution model.

- **#7825** - [Enhance Streamlit's Compatibility with Playwright on Windows](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/7825): Similar issue where Streamlit's event loop configuration conflicts with Playwright on Windows, requiring the Proactor event loop instead of Selector.

- **#6836** - [Provide async programming guide with streamlit](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/6836): Related request for official documentation and better support for asyncio patterns in Streamlit applications.

title: Bar chart does not display for one column data if there is a '.' in the column name
text: [CONTRIBUTOR] **If this issue affects you, please react with a 👍 (thumbs up emoji) to the initial post.** Your feedback helps us prioritize which bugs to investigate and address first. ![Views](https://api.views-badge.org/badge/st-issue-7714) [CONTRIBUTOR] Hey [USER]! Thank you for reporting this issue, I was able to reproduce it and can confirm that this is a bug. Issue demo link: https://issues.streamlit.app/?issue=gh-7714 [NONE] I can add to this that it also does not work for labels that contain square brackets, i.e. `"CO₂ Storage [t]"` [CONTRIBUTOR] This repros for all Altair-backed charts (bar, line, scatter, area), not just bar charts. This is because [the field parameter we pass in](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/38251aad1c2615ee8c100144f2e04eb9f26f1fd3/lib/streamlit/elements/arrow_altair.py#L1303) is sourced directly from the column name, [but _only_ for the non-"melted" case](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/38251aad1c2615ee8c100144f2e04eb9f26f1fd3/lib/streamlit/elements/arrow_altair.py#L1291-L1300), and we only "melt" [in the multi-column case](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/38251aad1c2615ee8c100144f2e04eb9f26f1fd3/lib/streamlit/elements/arrow_altair.py#L1208-L1227). The reason this breaks things is Altair treats string fields with dots as nested field access; see [these encoding docs](https://altair-viz.github.io/altair-viz-v4/user_guide/encoding.html): Note that the solution is a simple escape. [CONTRIBUTOR] Unsurprisingly this also breaks with brackets (e.g. `columns=["a[b]"]` in the example code).

title: Bar chart does not display for one column data if there is a '.' in the column name
text:
[CONTRIBUTOR] Unsurprisingly this also breaks with brackets (e.g. `columns=["a[b]"]` in the example code).

[CONTRIBUTOR] After playing around with this for a bit, escaping does _not_ seem to fix the underlying issue - at least for columns with dots in the name. There are also open bugs like [this one](https://github.com/vega/vega-lite/issues/7066) in vega-lite, which makes me think escaping simply isn't implemented correctly.

I think the right solution here is to use a uniqueified column name in all cases, not just the melted case. I'm going to unassign this until I have time to investigate that solution.

[COLLABORATOR] We don't have a concrete plan to work on this right now unfortunately. Would one of you be interested in working on a PR at some point? I'll bring it up with the team for discussion but I think at least exposing the basic types like `UploadedFile` in a separate namespace shouldn't be a controversial topic.

[COLLABORATOR] # Proposed solution

- Add a new module `streamlit.typing` (this is similar to what e.g. NumPy does, they have `numpy.typing`).
- This module should definitely contain `UploadedFile`. I couldn’t find anything else that should obviously be in there but might make sense to have another look through the library.
- What this should **not** contain:
    - `DeltaGenerator` → not clear if we want to keep this long-term, and there are no requests for it at the moment
    - Exceptions → these are already in `streamlit.errors`
- I think the `streamlit.typing` module should also be mentioned in the docs. We can start very small though and just use the existing docstrings for types (e.g. see [[here](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/c16232e330f084a9575ad54ab2dc78d6368df60c/lib/streamlit/runtime/uploaded_file_manager.py#L58)](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/c16232e330f084a9575ad54ab2dc78d6368df60c/lib/streamlit/runtime/uploaded_file_manager.py#L58) for UploadedFile).

Streamlit 1.62+ will expose various types/classes as part of the `streamlit.typing` namespace (also available as `st.typing`).

title: Enhance Streamlit's Compatibility with Playwright on Windows by Updating Event Loop Configuration
text:
Issue #7825: Enhance Streamlit's Compatibility with Playwright on Windows by Updating Event Loop Configuration
Labels: type:enhancement, area:windows

### Checklist

- [X] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar feature requests.
- [X] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

Streamlit's use of the older Selector event loop on Windows conflicts with Playwright's need for the newer Proactor event loop. This incompatibility causes exceptions when using Playwright for web scraping within Streamlit. The same issue will affect any other modules relying on the Proactor event loop in addition to Playwright.

### Why?

Playwright requires the Proactor event loop on Windows to run its driver in a subprocess, as the Selector event loop does not support async subprocesses. The Proactor event loop has replaced the Selector event loop as the default event loop on Windows starting with Python 3.8. The issue is [documented](https://playwright.dev/python/docs/library#incompatible-with-selectoreventloop-of-asyncio-on-windows) in Playwright's official documentation.

### How?

Proposing a modification or removal of the `_fix_tornado_crash` function in Streamlit ([source code](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/e4ab8f4578eac6c8b5ca4d518bf65f09849ea2b2/lib/streamlit/web/bootstrap.py#L406)). This function currently enforces the Selector event loop, which is incompatible with Playwright. An alternative solution could be introducing a configurable option for users to select the appropriate event loop.

### Additional Context

Tornado 6.1, released on October 30, 2020, supports the Proactor event loop on Windows (source: [Tornado 6.1 Release Notes](https://www.tornadoweb.org/en/stable/releases/v6.1.0.html)). Additionally, a related discussion in the Bokeh GitHub repository ([issue #12018](https://github.com/bokeh/bokeh/issues/12018)) and the [subsequent PR](https://github.com/bokeh/bokeh/pull/12019) supports the feasibility of this update.

Labels: type:bug, status:confirmed, priority:P3, feature:st.data_editor

### Checklist

- [X] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar issues.
- [X] I added a very descriptive title to this issue.

### Summary

Unlike `st.number_input`, `st.text_area`, and other widgets, `st.data_editor` only returns the input value after the user presses Enter or clicks outside the currently focused cell (excluding clicks on buttons).

### Reproducible Code Example

[![Open in Streamlit Cloud](https://static.streamlit.io/badges/streamlit_badge_black_white.svg)](https://issues.streamlitapp.com/?issue=gh-7868)

```Python
import pandas as pd
import streamlit as st


def set_state(i: int, df: pd.DataFrame) -> None:
    st.session_state.stage = i
    st.session_state.df = df


if "stage" not in st.session_state:
    st.session_state.stage = 0

if st.session_state.stage == 0:
    st.write("Input your data")
    df = st.data_editor(pd.DataFrame({"col1": ["a", "b"], "col2": ["c", "d"]}))
    st.button(
        "Begin",
        on_click=set_state,
        args=[1, df],
    )

if st.session_state.stage == 1:
    st.write("Your data")
    st.dataframe(st.session_state.df)
```

1. Click and edit a cell
2. Press the `Begin` button without clicking another area or pressing the Enter key.

title: `st.data_editor` doesn’t return the input value unless you press Enter or click outside the editor
text:
[COLLABORATOR] [USER]  Yep, that is a good idea. Maybe even just adding a very short delay (e.g. 10ms) for sending out the button trigger event would solve that as well.

[CONTRIBUTOR] Funnily enough I ran into this very problem not 10 minutes after posting last night 😂.

A short delay could work, though I think that makes some assumptions about the execution tike for all other elements on the page to update. For example, if I have a large dataframe in `data_editor`, is it possible the time the frontend needs to reassemble that into a rerun message potentially greater than 10ms? I don't know how you'd upper-bound that question...

I'm not very familiar with the frontend execution model but i think a delay would only reliably work if it's a "first-in-first-out" situation. I.e. when an element starts processing to emit a rerun request back to the server it aquires some lock which prevents other elements (e.g. button) from starting to process their own. Then a short delay might work in all scenarios because you only need to bound the time required for an element to _enter_ the processing of its rerun request, not the whole thing.

title: st.skeleton() - Implementation Proposal for space-filling empties.
text:
Issue #8032: st.skeleton() - Implementation Proposal for space-filling empties.
Labels: type:enhancement, feature:st.empty, type:possible-component, area:elements

### Checklist

- [X] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar feature requests.
- [X] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

I would like to work on adding a new container variation to Streamlit called `st.skeleton`. The `SkeletonElement` proto was added by [USER] in https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/7598 as a way to allow the Streamlit Scriptrunner to display a small loading animation while it was still waiting to start rendering elements to the page. However, at the time, no means was added to allow Streamlit app developers to use the new Skeleton element themselves.

This proposal outlines how _I_ think the new `st.skeleton` feature should function. It is also a call for discussion -- if you think this feature goes too far or not far enough, please let me know. If you would personally find a feature like this useful, please upvote.

### Why?

I think the Skeleton element has significant value as a way to allow app developers to separate -- both structurally and temporally -- the definition of their app's UI from the sometimes-IO-constrained process of fetching and rendering data. **an `st.skeleton` as defined in this proposal thus represents the promise of content to the end application user**

### How?

`st.skeleton` is fundamentally just an `st.empty` with a future promise of additional content (typically just one chart or plot or table or "thing" per skeleton)

### Call Signature

title: st.skeleton() - Implementation Proposal for space-filling empties.
text:
### How?

`st.skeleton` is fundamentally just an `st.empty` with a future promise of additional content (typically just one chart or plot or table or "thing" per skeleton)

### Call Signature

```python
st.skeleton(width=0.5, height=100, callback=my_function, autocallback=False)
# Width and height of the skeleton are configurable. Fractional values for width are treated as a percentage, 
# while values >1 are treated as a minimum pixel size.
```

### What does it look like?
See https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/7598
- May decide to add a third keywrod option to choose between an `AppSkeleton` and a `Skeleton` style animation but for now 

### What's the basic use case?
It's most basic use is a drop-in replacement for `st.empty()`. 
Like an empty, `st.skeleton()` returns a special SkeletonDeltaGenerator context manager object.
When you call another DeltaGenerator mixin function on it, it behaves just like an empty, and the skeleton animation that was playing is replaced by the new content. So this

```python
# Draw UI
st.write("Census Data")
census_data_placeholder = st.empty()  # The empty is a collapsed element
year = st.selectbox("Select Year", options=[2022, 2023, 2024])

# Get data from source
# assume function call takes a long time
census_dataframe = get_census_data_from_database(year)

# Draw the data, causing it to "pop" in above the year selectbox.
census_data_placeholder.dataframe(census_dataframe)
```

becomes

title: st.skeleton() - Implementation Proposal for space-filling empties.
text:
becomes

```python
# Draw UI
st.write("Census Data")
census_data_placeholder = st.skeleton(height=500px)  # The skeleton holds space for the future data
year = st.selectbox("Select Year", options=[2022, 2023, 2024])

# Get data from source, assume this takes a long time
census_dataframe = get_census_data_from_database(year)

# Draw the data, replacing the skeleton animation that was previously there
census_data_placeholder.dataframe(census_dataframe)
```

In this case (and as you will see below, in this case only) replacement can happen multiple times:

```python
skeleton = st.skeleton()

# User is shown a skeleton animation while data1 loads
data1 = get_data_long_running_function()
skeleton.dataframe(data1)

# User sees data1 while data2 loads, then data1 is replaced
data2 = get_data_another_long_running_function()
skeleton.dataframe(data2)
```

### Use as a context manager
When you use `st.skeleton()` in a `with` statement, it first places an `st.container` inside of itself
and then sets that as the DeltaGenerator context, allowing you to write natural code like:

```python
# Draw UI
st.write("Census Data")
census_data_placeholder = st.skeleton(height=500px)
year = st.selectbox("Select Year", options=[2022, 2023, 2024])

# Get data from source, assume this takes a long time
census_dataframe = get_census_data_from_database(year)
census_statistics = compute_statistics(census_dataframe)

# Draw the data, replacing the skeleton animation that was previously there
# Both the st.dataframe and the st.write are dispalyed inside of an st.container
# inside of the skeleton
with census_data_placeholder:
    st.dataframe(census_dataframe)
    st.write(census_statistics)
```

title: st.skeleton() - Implementation Proposal for space-filling empties.
text:
If only implemented up to this point in the proposal `st.skeleton` is still useful as a way to have an `st.empty` take up space in a page's UI. This avoids "pop-in" data that changes the layout of the UI significantly for the end user -- which is a problem that can currently happen with `st.empty`

### Getting fancy with callbacks
Going beyond basic `st.empty` functionality, `st.skeleton` also has a `callback` argument which allows you to queue up some function to be run at a later time. The callback function is assumed to itself call into one or more Streamlit elements. It can be run directly by calling `.load(*args, **kwargs)` on the `SkeletonDeltaGenerator`. The callback function acts as if it were being run inside a `with skeleton:` block, e.g.

```python
skeleton = st.skeleton(callback=my_function)
# ... more code
skeleton.load(a, b, c)
```

is equivalent to

```python
skeleton = st.skeleton()
# ... more code
with skeleton:
   my_function(a, b, c)
```

As an example:

```python
def render_census_data(year):
    # Get data from source, assume this takes a long time
    census_dataframe = get_census_data_from_database(year)
    census_statistics = compute_statistics(census_dataframe)
    # Draw the data
    st.dataframe(census_dataframe)
    st.write(census_statistics)

# Draw UI
st.write("Census Data")
census_data_placeholder = st.skeleton(height=500px, callback=render_census_data)
year = st.selectbox("Select Year", options=[2022, 2023, 2024])

# Load the census data and display it in place of the skeleton by running
# the callback function.
census_data_placeholder.load(year)
```

title: st.skeleton() - Implementation Proposal for space-filling empties.
text:
### Lions and Tigers and Autocallbacks, Oh my!
Where callbacks can _really_ shine is via an "autocallback" feature. This is a user-configurable feature which is enabled
by default. When an `st.skeleton()` call with a callback function is encountered, it will register itself with the current `ScriptRunner`. At the end of a successful and complete page execution, the ScriptRunner will then call `.load()` on all of the `SkeletonDeltaGenerator`s that meet the following criteria:
1. the `.load()` method was not already called on them by the user
2. they have a valid element path on the front end (meaning they haven't been _replaced_ by any other content yet)

`.load()` is called in the order that the `st.skeleton()` was first encountered. There may be additional limitations (such as enforcing that callback functions do not modify session_state or something like that.

When autocallback is enabled (by default), the st.skeleton() also accepts `args` and `kwargs` parameters since
there will be no calling of the `load` function.

```python
# Draw UI
st.write("Census Data")
year = st.selectbox("Select Year", options=[2022, 2023, 2024])
census_data_placeholder = st.skeleton(height=500px, callback=render_census_data, args=[year])

# The callback render_census_data is automatically called at the end of script execution with the argument `year`
```

Optional: the SkeletonDeltaGenerator also has a `.set_callback_arguments(*args, **kwargs)` method so that parameters
can be set even after the SkeletonDeltaGenerator is created

```python
# Draw UI
st.write("Census Data")
census_data_placeholder = st.skeleton(height=500px, callback=render_census_data)
year = st.selectbox("Select Year", options=[2022, 2023, 2024])
census_data_placeholder.set_callback_args(year)
```

title: st.skeleton() - Implementation Proposal for space-filling empties.
text:
Optional: the SkeletonDeltaGenerator also has a `.set_callback_arguments(*args, **kwargs)` method so that parameters
can be set even after the SkeletonDeltaGenerator is created

```python
# Draw UI
st.write("Census Data")
census_data_placeholder = st.skeleton(height=500px, callback=render_census_data)
year = st.selectbox("Select Year", options=[2022, 2023, 2024])
census_data_placeholder.set_callback_args(year)
```

And you can turn it off via a global config option or a keyword argument

```python
census_data_placeholder = st.skeleton(height=500px, callback=render_census_data, autocallback=False)
```

So, if we get to an agreement on adding this to Streamlit, I'm pretty sure that we will want to ship - at least in the initial release - only with the `height` parameter. I think `height` has a significant benefit since we can lower some jumping effects since the developer can reserve space on the UI based on what he knows will render there.
